meta.blurb: At dusk the dragon Vessa breathes out to light the harbour beacon, and only smoke comes. A boy named Tam helps her climb a snowy pass to find her fire. A storm is coming, and someone wants the light to stay dark.
meta.bible: Vessa: a dragon the colour of deep sea water, blue-green scales and golden eyes; gentle, proud and secretly afraid of her own fire; came to Saltmere the year Tam was born and lights the Great Beacon every dusk. Tam Brightwater: twelve years old, brave and kind, lives at the beacon with his grandfather, brings Vessa a mackerel every morning, carries a candle. Corran Brightwater: Tam's grandfather, the quiet keeper of the Great Beacon, weathered hands, wise and steady. Nan Tern: Old Nan Tern, the sharp-eyed keeper of the town's stories; knows about the Ember Pool. Captain Drusk: a thin man in a long dark coat who earns his living from wrecks; plots to wreck the grain ship by putting out the beacon and hanging false lanterns on the Teeth. Berrin Oakes: a Saltmere fisherman whose boat nearly hits the Teeth. Gannet: the grain ship that comes home in the Harvest Storm. Saltmere: the harbour town. Gull Head: the headland with the Great Beacon, a stone tower with a huge iron bowl. The Teeth: the line of black rocks beyond the harbour mouth. Mount Karrow: the mountain where Vessa's cave and the Ember Pool are. Whispering Marsh: the foggy marsh with false pale lights. Ember Pool: a hidden lake of liquid light deep inside Mount Karrow where dragon fire was first born. Harvest Storm: the great autumn storm. Facts: a dragon's fire never dies, it only hides when the dragon is afraid; eleven years ago, in her first week, a gust of wind threw Vessa's flames across the harbour and burned the fishing sheds, nets and winter stores, and nobody was hurt; the town forgave her, but she never forgave herself and kept her fire small until it faded; without fire her wings grow stiff and she grows cold; the journey to the Ember Pool takes three days on foot. Voice and tone: warm, adventurous and a little funny, a fantasy for readers of every age; danger is real but never gory; the theme is forgiving yourself and using your gifts bravely.

beats.scene: A boy and an old man climb the spiral stairs inside a stone tower
beats.summary: Tam, twelve years old, lives with his grandfather Corran, who keeps the Great Beacon.

beats.scene: A huge blue-green dragon breathes golden fire into a beacon bowl at dusk
beats.summary: Every dusk the dragon Vessa lights the beacon with a river of golden fire.

beats.scene: Black rocks like teeth stick out of the sea beyond the harbour mouth
beats.summary: The Teeth, a line of sharp rocks beyond the harbour, make the beacon vital to the town.

beats.scene: Tam hands a silver fish to the dragon on the headland at sunrise
beats.summary: Tam and Vessa are friends; he brings her a fish every morning.

beats.scene: Vessa on the tower breathes out only a thin grey puff of smoke
beats.summary: One autumn dusk Vessa breathes at the beacon, and only smoke comes out.

beats.scene: Vessa tries again beside the dark bowl, then flies off into the night
beats.summary: Vessa tries again and fails, then flies away to Mount Karrow, and Corran lights the old oil lamp.

beats.scene: Fishing boats creep through dark water while a thin man watches from the quay
beats.summary: The fleet comes home by the weak lamp, one boat nearly hits the Teeth, and Captain Drusk smiles.

beats.summary: Tam finds Vessa cold and shaking in her cave, and she admits that her fire is gone.

beats.scene: Vessa lowers her great head to tell Tam how her fire faded
beats.summary: Vessa says her fire faded for weeks and that she hid it from everyone.

beats.scene: Tam holds a candle in front of Vessa's nose, and nothing happens
beats.summary: Tam tests her with a candle, finds the fire truly gone, and promises to help.

beats.scene: An old woman in a shawl sits by a cottage fire, knitting and listening
beats.summary: Tam asks Old Nan Tern, the town's keeper of stories, about dragons and fire.

beats.scene: Vessa stares out of the cave at the sea, remembering burning sheds

beats.scene: Tam sits beside Vessa's great head and speaks with a steady voice
beats.summary: Tam says the town forgave her long ago, and Vessa agrees to go to the Ember Pool.

beats.scene: Corran hands Tam a lantern and a bundle of food in the cottage doorway
beats.summary: Tam tells Corran, who gives him a lantern and promises to keep the oil lamp burning.

beats.scene: Tam and Vessa walk side by side along a dark road
beats.summary: Tam and Vessa set out for the Ember Pool on foot, because without fire Vessa's wings are stiff.

beats.scene: Fog hangs over a wet marsh with pale lights floating above the water
beats.summary: In the Whispering Marsh, thick fog and false lights confuse them, and Vessa cannot burn the fog away.

beats.scene: Tam walks ahead holding a lantern, with a rope tied to Vessa behind him
beats.summary: Tam ties a rope to Vessa and leads her along the old marker posts across the marsh.

beats.scene: A shivering dragon rests beside a small campfire on a river bank

beats.scene: Vessa watches the small flames with wary golden eyes
beats.summary: Vessa tells Tam what it is like to have no fire, and she watches the flames carefully.

beats.scene: A dragon pushes a huge boulder aside in a narrow rocky gorge
beats.summary: In a gorge blocked by fallen rocks, Vessa uses her great strength to clear the way.

beats.scene: A boy and a dragon shelter in a rock crack as snow blows past
beats.summary: A snowstorm on the high pass forces them to shelter in a crack in the cliff, where they share bread and warmth.

beats.scene: Under bright stars a boy sits against a dragon's side and talks quietly

beats.scene: A dark tunnel mouth in a cliff face glows faintly orange from inside
beats.summary: On the third morning they find a tunnel in the cliff with a faint glow deep inside.

beats.scene: A dark harbour seen from above, with small lights on the rocks

beats.summary: The fleet and the Gannet steer towards the false lights, fooled by the trap.

beats.summary: Vessa lands at the beacon, and Tam finds the smashed lamp and frees his grandfather.

beats.scene: Corran points toward the sea as Vessa stares at the empty beacon bowl
beats.summary: Corran says Drusk did it; Vessa is frightened, because the beacon needs a great flame.

beats.scene: A dragon and a boy with a candle climb a windy tower
beats.summary: Tam stands beside Vessa and tells her to light the beacon one breath at a time.

beats.scene: A huge golden flame roars into the great beacon bowl and lights the sea
beats.summary: Vessa lights the beacon with a great, steady flame that stays inside the bowl.

beats.scene: Sailors on pitching boats stare at a bright beacon high on the headland
beats.summary: The fleet sees the true light and turns away from the Teeth.

beats.scene: A dragon swoops low over black rocks as men in a boat flee
beats.summary: Vessa flies to the Teeth and scares off the wreckers with a controlled ring of fire.

beats.summary: All the boats and the Gannet reach the harbour safely, and Saltmere cheers.

beats.summary: The townsfolk catch Drusk and his men, and the town tells Vessa that she was forgiven long ago.

beats.scene: A boy and a dragon light the beacon together at sunset
beats.summary: Vessa lights the beacon every dusk with Tam beside her, and her fire is gentle, bright and steady.

A1A2: At dusk, the fishing boats came home to the town of Saltmere.
A boy named Tam lived at the beacon with his grandfather.
Every night, the dragon Vessa lit the beacon with her fire.
Hidden rocks called the Teeth waited near the harbour for lost boats.
Each morning, Tam brought Vessa a fish, and they talked together.
One autumn evening, Vessa breathed out, but only smoke came.
She tried again and failed, and then she flew away.
The boats came home late, and one almost hit the rocks.
At dawn, Tam climbed the mountain with fish for Vessa.
Vessa lay cold in her cave and told Tam her fire was gone.
Vessa said her fire had been getting smaller for many weeks.
Tam held a candle, and Vessa blew, but nothing happened.
Tam went to see Old Nan Tern, who knew many old stories.
Nan told Tam about a magic pool deep inside the mountain.
Nan said, “A dragon's fire never dies, but it can hide.”
Vessa told Tam how her fire once burned the harbour sheds.
Tam said the town was not angry now, and she agreed to go.
Corran gave Tam a lantern and said, “Come home safely.”
Tam and Vessa walked away from the sea toward the mountains.
In the marsh, the fog was thick and they could not see.
Tam tied a rope to Vessa and led her through the marsh.
Vessa swam across the river and was very cold afterwards.
Vessa watched the small fire and spoke about her fear.
Rocks had fallen across the path, so Vessa pushed them away.
Snow fell on the mountain, and they hid in a small cave.
At night, Tam told Vessa about his mother, a sailor.
In the morning, they found a dark door in the mountain.
Inside was a great cave with a pool of glowing light.
In the water, Vessa saw herself as a young dragon.
A voice said, “Your fire is still here, behind a door.”
Vessa said, “I am afraid my fire will hurt people.”
Tam said, “Your fire has saved many boats.”
Vessa tried to breathe fire, and a little spark came out.
Tam held up a candle, and Vessa lit it with her fire.
Her wings felt warm again, and she practised making fire.
In Saltmere, Captain Drusk made a bad plan with his men.
Drusk's men locked Corran in the cellar and broke the lamp.
Drusk's men put false lights on the rocks in the storm.
Vessa flew fast over the mountains, with Tam on her back.
They saw no light on the tower, only strange lights on the rocks.
The boats saw the false lights and turned toward the rocks.
Tam found his grandfather locked in the cellar and let him out.
Corran said Drusk had done it, and the boats were in danger.
Tam said, “I am here, Vessa, and you can do it.”
Vessa breathed out, and a big golden fire filled the bowl.
The sailors saw the true light and turned away from the rocks.
Vessa flew to the rocks and made Drusk's men run away.
All the boats came home safely, and the town cheered loudly.
The people caught Drusk, and they thanked Vessa for her light.
Every night after that, Vessa lit the beacon with Tam beside her.
B1B2: Every evening the fishing boats of Saltmere sail home as the sun goes down. High on Gull Head stands the Great Beacon, a stone tower with a huge iron bowl waiting to be lit.
Tam Brightwater is twelve years old, and he lives in the cottage at the foot of the beacon. His grandfather Corran is the keeper, and he sweeps the tower and cares for it every day.
Every evening the dragon Vessa glides down from the hills and lands on top of the tower. She breathes a river of golden fire into the iron bowl, and the whole bay glows with light.
Beyond the harbour mouth lies a line of sharp black rocks that the fishermen call the Teeth. In the dark they are deadly, and only the beacon shows the safe way past them.
Vessa came to Saltmere in the year that Tam was born, and the two of them are close friends. Every morning he climbs the headland with a fresh mackerel, and they talk until the sun is high.
One autumn evening Vessa settles on the tower, takes a deep breath, and blows at the bowl. Instead of golden fire, a thin grey curl of smoke drifts out, and the iron stays dark.
Vessa tries a second time, and then a third, but nothing comes except a cough. Without a word she spreads her wings and flies towards Mount Karrow, while Corran hurries to light the old oil lamp.
That night the fishing fleet feels its way home by the weak glow of the lamp. Berrin Oakes's boat scrapes past the Teeth by a hair, and on the quay Captain Drusk watches with a thin smile.
At first light Tam takes a bucket of fish and sets off up the path to Mount Karrow. He knows that dragons hide when they are hurt, and he knows which cave is hers.
Tam finds Vessa curled up at the back of her cave, shivering from nose to tail. In a small, broken voice she tells him the truth, which is that her fire has gone out.
Vessa tells him that her fire has been fading for weeks, a little more each night. She has told no one, because she is afraid that the town will stop needing her.
Tam holds an unlit candle in front of her nose and asks her to try one very small breath. Nothing happens, and as she looks away in shame, Tam promises that he will help her find the cause.
Back in town, Tam goes to see Old Nan Tern, who knows more stories than anyone in Saltmere. He tells her only that a friend has lost something precious, and he asks about dragons and fire.
Nan tells him that deep inside Mount Karrow lies the Ember Pool, where the first dragon fire was born. Every dragon's flame is a piece of it, and a dragon who is ill can go there to be healed.
Nan adds a warning, that a dragon's fire does not simply vanish like a candle in the wind. It hides when something frightens the dragon, so he should ask his friend what she fears.

Tam asks the question, and after a long silence Vessa tells him a story he has never heard. In her first week at Saltmere, her flames raged out of control and burned all the fishing sheds on the quay.
Tam tells her that the whole town forgave her a long time ago. Vessa cannot quite believe it, but she agrees to go to the Ember Pool, because the fleet needs her light.

Tam tells his grandfather everything, and Corran listens in silence before he gives his blessing. He packs a lantern, bread and a blanket, and he promises to keep the old lamp burning until they return.
They set out that same evening, and Vessa walks beside Tam along the old road. Her wings are stiff and cold without her fire, so she cannot fly far, and the journey will be long.

By the second night they reach the Whispering Marsh, where thick white fog hangs over the black water. Strange pale lights float in the mist, and Vessa cannot burn it away as she once would have done.

Tam ties a rope around his waist and the other end to Vessa, and he leads the way with his lantern. He ignores the pale lights and follows the old wooden posts one by one until the ground is firm again.

Next morning they come to a wide, icy river, and Vessa swims across because she is too big for the stepping stones. On the far bank she shakes with cold, so Tam lights a small fire and wraps her in a blanket.
Vessa stares at the little flames for a long time without speaking. She says that having no fire feels like an empty, dark room inside her, yet she is also afraid of flames.
Beyond the river the path enters a narrow gorge, where many rocks have fallen across the way. Vessa has lost her fire but not her strength, and she pushes the great stones aside one by one.
High on the pass a snowstorm blows in from the north and nearly knocks Tam off his feet. They squeeze into a crack in the rock, and Vessa curls around him to keep the cold away.
When the storm passes, the stars come out, and Tam begins to talk about his mother. She was a sailor who was lost in a storm one dark night, long before Vessa came to Saltmere.
On the third morning they find a narrow opening in the cliff, half hidden by ice and old stones. A faint orange glow shines from deep inside, and warm air drifts out against their faces.
The tunnel leads down into a vast cavern, and in the middle lies the Ember Pool. Its water shines like melted gold, and warm mist rises from it and fills the air with a smell of hot stone.
Vessa steps to the edge of the pool and looks down into the glowing water. She sees no reflection of herself, only a young dragon and burning sheds, and she turns away with a cry.
A deep, kind voice seems to rise from the water and fill the whole cave. It tells Vessa that her fire is not lost, but is locked behind a door that she closed herself.
Vessa takes a long breath and says the words out loud, even though her voice shakes. She fears that her fire will hurt someone again, and for years she has kept it small and tight.
Tam reminds her of every night that her fire has brought the fishing boats safely home. He says that fire can hurt, but it is also light and warmth, and it tells people that someone cares.
Vessa closes her eyes, breathes in slowly, and tries again while Tam holds his breath. A tiny golden spark flies from her nose and glows for a moment, but it dies before it can grow.
Tam holds the candle up in front of her nose, as he did in the cave. Vessa breathes out very softly, and a small, steady flame leaps onto the wick and begins to burn.
Warmth spreads through Vessa from nose to tail, and her stiff wings begin to move freely again. All that day she practises, making her flame a little bigger each time, while Tam sits and counts.
Meanwhile, in Saltmere, Captain Drusk is talking with his men in a dim room above the quay. A big storm is coming, and a rich grain ship with it, and Drusk means the beacon to stay dark.
On the night the storm arrives, Drusk's men push their way into the beacon tower. They lock old Corran in the cellar and smash the oil lamp, and the last light on Gull Head goes out.
Out in the rising wind, Drusk and his men row to the Teeth and hang lanterns on the rocks. The false lights will look like the safe channel to any sailor who cannot see the real one.
Far away in the mountains, Vessa spreads her wings, and Tam climbs onto her back. They fly fast across the land towards the sea, with the storm clouds racing close behind them.
As the coast comes into view, Tam sees that the great beacon is dark. Out on the Teeth, a crooked line of small lights shines through the rain, and he knows that something is wrong.

Out on the wild water, the fishing fleet and the grain ship Gannet see the lights and turn towards them. The sailors think that they are heading for the safe channel, but they are sailing straight onto the rocks.
Vessa lands on the headland, and Tam jumps down and runs into the tower. He finds the smashed lamp, hears knocking, and pulls back the heavy bolt on the cellar door.
Corran tells them that Drusk is behind the plot, and that the boats will reach the rocks in minutes. Vessa looks at the huge iron bowl and trembles, because it needs a flame that is big and bold.
Tam climbs the tower beside Vessa, shielding his little candle from the wind with his coat. He tells her that she does not have to be brave all at once, only for one breath at a time.
Vessa closes her eyes, takes a huge breath, and lets it out in a great river of golden fire. The flame fills the iron bowl and stays there, roaring and steady, and the whole bay lights up.
Far out at sea, the sailors see the great beacon burst into flame and stare in wonder. They know that light at once, and they swing their boats away from the false lanterns and into the safe channel.
Vessa swoops down to the Teeth and breathes a ring of fire in the air in front of Drusk's boat. The wreckers cry out in terror, throw down their oars, and beg for mercy.
One by one, the fishing boats and the grain ship Gannet slide through the channel into the calm harbour. The whole town is waiting on the quay, and when the last boat arrives, a great cheer goes up.

The fishermen of Saltmere seize Drusk and his men as soon as their boat touches the quay. Then the people gather around Vessa and tell her that she was forgiven long ago and has been loved ever since.

From that night on, Vessa lights the beacon every evening, and Tam stands beside her as the assistant keeper. Her fire is bright, steady and gentle, and on cold mornings she warms the bakers' ovens for the whole town.
C1C2: The little harbour town of Saltmere lay in the last gold light of the day, and its fishing boats were hurrying home across the grey water with their sails full of wind. On the headland above, the Great Beacon stood tall and dark, an iron bowl on a tower of stone, waiting for the one flame that could bring them safely in. Every sailor in the fleet watched it, because everyone knew that the sea along that coast was kind to no one who lost his way.

Tam Brightwater was twelve years old, and he had lived all his life in the stone cottage at the foot of the beacon with his grandfather Corran. Corran was the keeper of the tower, a quiet man with weathered hands who swept its stairs, polished its great bowl and watched the weather the way other people watch the faces of their friends. Tam helped him every day, and he could not think of a better place in the world to grow up.

Vessa was a dragon the colour of deep sea water, with scales that flashed green and blue and a pair of wings as wide as a fishing boat is long. At dusk each day she settled lightly upon the tower, drew in a slow breath, and let out a river of golden fire that woke the great bowl in a single roar. The light poured across the bay, and the people of Saltmere, who had watched it a thousand times, still stopped what they were doing to look.

Just beyond the harbour mouth lay a ragged row of black rocks that the fishermen called the Teeth, and they had swallowed more ships than anyone had counted. On a clear day they were a harmless curiosity, but on a moonless night or in a screaming gale they were death waiting with its mouth open. Without the beacon, no captain could have found the narrow, safe channel between them, and the town knew it.

Vessa had come to Saltmere in the year that Tam was born, and in all the time since, the boy and the dragon had grown into the closest of friends. Every morning he climbed the headland with a fresh mackerel in a bucket, and every morning she pretended to be surprised, although she had smelled it from a mile away. They talked about the weather, the gulls and the strange ways of people, and neither of them ever ran out of things to say.

One evening in the autumn, Vessa landed on the tower as she had done a thousand times before, drew in a breath that made her whole body swell, and let it go. What came out was not a river of golden fire but a thin, grey wisp of smoke that curled once in the wind and was gone. In the silence that followed, Tam, who was standing at the bottom of the stairs, felt his heart turn cold.

She tried again, and then again, and each time the only answer was a dry cough and a smell of cold ash. Then, without a word to Tam or to anyone, she flung herself off the tower and flew heavily away towards Mount Karrow, her wings beating as if they were made of lead. Corran, who understood at once what was at stake, climbed the stairs with the old oil lamp in his hand and lit it, though its glow was pitifully small against the night.

That night the fishing fleet crept home by the feeble light of the oil lamp, and every sailor held his breath as the black rocks slid past. Berrin Oakes's boat came so close to the Teeth that its keel screamed against the stone, and only a shout from the stern kept it off the worst of them. On the quay, wrapped in a long dark coat, Captain Drusk watched the near disaster, and the corner of his mouth lifted in something that was not quite a smile.

Before the sun was properly up, Tam filled a bucket with mackerel, slung a rope over his shoulder and set off along the stony goat path that wound up the side of Mount Karrow. Vessa had once shown him her hiding place, a deep cave high on the slope, and he had a feeling that she would not be anywhere else. The path was steep and the wind was cold, but he climbed without stopping, for he could think of nothing but the look on her face the night before.

He found her at the very back of the cave, curled around herself like a cat on a cold night, and her scales, which usually glowed with warmth, were as cold to the touch as river stones. When he spoke her name she raised her great head slowly, and the look in her golden eyes was one that he had never seen there before. “It is gone,” she whispered, and the words sounded like a crack in glass, “and I do not know where.”

It had begun many weeks ago, she explained, with flames that came out smaller and paler each evening, until the last few nights when she had been breathing out little more than warm air. She had hidden it from everyone, even from Tam, because a dragon who cannot make fire is only a very large animal with a great deal of appetite. Her fear, she admitted, was that Saltmere would look at her one day and wonder what she was for.

Tam took a candle from his pocket, held it up in front of her great nostrils, and asked her to try the smallest breath she could manage. She tried, and there was only a gust of cool air that made the wick sway and nothing more, and a tear the size of a plum rolled down her cheek. Tam laid his hand against her cold neck and promised, with all the seriousness a twelve-year-old can find, that he would not rest until he had found her fire again.

Tam hurried down the mountain to the cottage of Old Nan Tern, who was said to know more stories than there were fish in the bay. He did not give away Vessa's secret, but he told her that a friend had lost something precious, and he asked what the old tales said about dragons and their fire. Nan, who had sharp eyes and a sharper mind, put down her knitting and looked at him for a long moment before she answered.

Deep inside Mount Karrow, Nan told him, lay the Ember Pool, a hidden lake of liquid light where the first dragon fire was born when the world was young. Every dragon's flame was said to be a small spark of that ancient glow, kept burning by the creature's own heart, and a dragon whose flame had faltered might go there to be made whole. The way was long and hard, and few had found it in a hundred years.

Then Nan leaned forward and said something that he would remember for the rest of his life, that a true dragon's fire never goes out and can only be hidden. It hides when its owner is afraid, she explained, folding itself away like a frightened animal in a burrow, and no cure will work until the fear itself is faced. If his friend wished to be whole again, Tam should ask her, gently and plainly, what it was that she dreaded most.

Tam asked what she feared, and after a long silence Vessa told him a story that he had never heard in all his twelve years. In her first week at Saltmere, a gust of wind had thrown her flames across the harbour and set the fishing sheds alight, and the nets and winter stores had all been lost. Nobody had been hurt, and the people had rebuilt and forgiven her, but she had never forgiven herself, and ever since she had breathed her fire small, careful and tight.

Tam told her, as firmly as he could, that Saltmere had forgiven her long before he could walk, and that nobody there thought of the old fire except her. Vessa listened with her eyes closed and said nothing for so long that he feared he had said the wrong thing. At last she opened them and agreed that they would go to the Ember Pool together, not because she believed him yet, but because the fleet could not go on trusting a feeble lamp.

Tam told his grandfather the whole story, and Corran listened in silence, rubbing his chin, before he said that a boy who keeps faith with a friend was worth more than any lamp. He packed a lantern, a loaf, a blanket and a coil of rope, and promised that the old oil lamp would burn every night until they came home. Then, almost as an afterthought, he mentioned that Captain Drusk had been asking a great many questions about how long the dragon would be away.

They set out together that very evening, the boy with his lantern and the great dragon padding silently beside him along the old road that led away from the sea. Without her fire, Vessa found that her wings had grown stiff and heavy, and she could manage no more than a short, clumsy glide at a time. It would have to be a journey on foot, and Tam, glancing up at the huge shape in the dark, was glad of her company all the same.

On the second night they came to the Whispering Marsh, a flat and ghostly country where the fog lay so thick that Tam could scarcely see his own boots. Pale lights drifted over the black water, inviting the traveller to follow them into the bog, and in the old days Vessa would simply have burned the mist away with one sweep of her flame. Now she could only stand and tremble, and the shame of it hurt her more than the cold.

Tam, who had grown up beside a light that guided strangers to safety, knew better than to trust one that did not. He tied one end of the rope about his waist and the other about Vessa's neck, held his lantern high, and followed the old wooden marker posts one by one, ignoring the lights that whispered from the dark. By the time the grey dawn arrived they were standing on solid ground, wet to the knees and laughing with relief.

The next morning they reached a wide, icy river, and since Vessa was far too big for the stepping stones she swam across, snorting at the cold. On the far bank she lay on the gravel, shaking so hard that her teeth rattled, because a dragon without fire has no furnace inside to defend her against the water. Tam gathered driftwood, struck a spark with his flint, and in a few minutes there was a small, crackling fire, with the blanket tucked around her like a tent.

Vessa stared at the little flames for a long time, and the light danced in her great golden eyes. She told Tam that having no fire felt like living in a house where every lamp had been blown out, and that the strangest part was that she both longed for it and dreaded it. Tam said nothing, because he had a feeling that she was finally saying aloud something that she had never said to anyone.

Beyond the river the road narrowed into a gorge so steep that the sky was only a ribbon overhead, and a slide of boulders had fallen across it in the last spring rains. Vessa put her shoulder to the largest, and with a groan that echoed from wall to wall she rolled it aside as easily as a child rolls a ball. Tam cheered, and she lifted her head a little higher, for it was the first time in weeks that anyone had needed her strength.

Near the top of the pass, a snowstorm rushed in from the north with a howl, and the wind plucked at Tam's coat as though it wanted to carry him off the mountain. They found a crack in the cliff, just wide enough for the two of them, and Vessa curled her great body around the boy like a wall. For once it was the dragon who kept the human warm, and the two of them shared the last of the bread in the dark.

When the storm had blown itself out, the stars appeared, sharp and white, and Tam found himself talking about his mother, whom he could barely remember. She had been a sailor, he said, and she had been lost in a storm on a night when the old beacon fire was blown out by the gale, a year before Vessa arrived. That was why he loved the light so much, he said, and why he could not bear to think of it ever going dark again.

On the morning of the third day, they found a narrow opening in the cliff, half hidden behind curtains of ice, and from somewhere deep inside came a faint orange glow. A breath of warm air rolled out to meet them, the first real warmth that Vessa had felt in weeks, and she closed her eyes and let it wash over her. Neither of them spoke, because both of them knew that they had arrived at the place the old stories described.

The tunnel wound down and down until it opened into a cavern so vast that the lantern light could not reach its roof, and in the middle of the cavern lay the Ember Pool. Its surface glowed like melted gold, and slow ribbons of warm mist rose from it and hung in the air, smelling of hot stone and distant summers. Tam stood speechless at the edge, and he felt Vessa trembling beside him, though no longer from cold.

Vessa stepped to the edge of the pool and looked down, but the glowing water did not show her the dragon she was now. It showed her instead a young and frightened creature standing on a quay, with smoke rolling up from a row of burning sheds behind her, and she turned her head away with a cry that echoed around the cavern. Tam put his hand on her neck and told her softly that she did not have to look for long.

Then a voice, deep and gentle and old, seemed to rise from the water and fill the cavern, and it spoke to Vessa in a language that she understood without having learned it. “Your fire is not lost,” it said, “but resting behind a door that you shut yourself, and only you can open it again.” “The door will open,” it added, “when you can say aloud what you fear and mean every word.”

Vessa drew a long breath, lifted her head, and said the words aloud for the first time in eleven years. She was afraid, she told the empty cavern, that her fire would hurt someone again, and so for all that time she had held it small and tight and quiet until it had forgotten how to be anything else. As she spoke, something seemed to loosen in her chest, like a knot being gently untied.

Tam stood in front of her and spoke the way Corran spoke when something truly mattered, slowly and without any decoration. He reminded her of every stormy night when her flame had guided the boats safely home, of every winter when she had warmed the frozen quay, and of every child who had slept trusting her light. One mistake, he told her, did not cancel a thousand gifts, and the people she was so afraid of hurting had forgiven her before she had even forgiven herself.

She closed her eyes and drew in a slow breath, and this time something answered, a faint heat deep inside her like the first stirring of a banked stove. A single golden spark leapt from her nostrils and hung in the air between them, glowing bravely for a moment before it went dark. Vessa opened her eyes in despair, but Tam was grinning, because he had seen with his own eyes that the spark was real.

Tam took the candle from his pocket and held it up before her, just as he had in her cave days earlier, and said nothing at all. Vessa breathed out slowly, as softly as someone blowing on a cup of tea, and a small gold flame stepped out of her mouth and settled upon the wick as if it had always belonged there. For a moment neither of them could speak, and then Vessa laughed and wept at the same time while the light of one little candle danced across the cavern roof.

Warmth spread through her from nose to tail, and her stiff wings unfolded and began to move as freely as they had in her youth. All through that day she practised in the great cavern, making her flame a little larger each time and always gathering it back before it could wander. Tam sat on a rock and kept count, and when the pool glowed brighter than ever, they both knew that it was time to go home.

Meanwhile in Saltmere, Captain Drusk sat with his crew of salvagers in a dim room above the quay, and they were counting days. The dragon had gone, the old lamp was weak, and a great autumn storm that the sailors called the Harvest Storm was due within the week, bringing the grain ship Gannet home with a hold full of rich cargo. A ship that wrecked on the Teeth would scatter its goods along the shore for anyone bold enough to gather them, and Drusk had long dreamed of such a night.

When the first black clouds of the Harvest Storm rolled over the sea, Drusk's men marched up Gull Head and burst into the tower while the old keeper was still lighting his lamp. They seized Corran, who fought them as best he could with a broom, and shut him in the cellar behind a heavy bolt, and one of them smashed the lamp on the stone floor. The last light on the headland went out, and the whole coast turned black.

Out in the rising gale, Drusk and his men rowed to the Teeth with a boatload of lanterns and hung them in a crooked line along the rocks. To a sailor struggling home through the darkness, those lights would look exactly like the entrance to the safe channel, and he would steer for them with all the hope in his heart. It was a cruel and clever trick, and Drusk laughed softly as the wind tore at his coat.

Far away in the mountains, Vessa spread her newly warmed wings, and Tam scrambled onto her back and gripped the ridge of her neck with both hands. She leapt from the cavern's mouth and soared over ridge and gorge and marsh, faster than she had flown in years, while the wind roared past them and the storm clouds chased them like hounds. Tam shouted with joy and terror together, and he had never in his life felt so alive.

When the coast came into sight, Tam saw with a sinking heart that Gull Head was black, with not even the little oil lamp burning in its window. Out on the Teeth, however, a crooked line of small bright lights was glittering through the rain, in exactly the place where no lights should ever be. He understood in an instant that somebody had done this on purpose, and that the fleet was sailing blind into a trap.

Out on the heaving water, the weary fishermen of Saltmere and the crew of the grain ship Gannet saw the lights on the Teeth and thanked their luck, for they believed that they were being shown the way home. One by one the boats turned their bows toward the false lanterns, riding the huge swells, and every minute carried them closer to the rocks that were waiting beneath the foam. Only the dragon, wheeling high above, could see how little time there was left.

Vessa dropped onto the headland, and Tam slid from her back and ran into the tower, where the first thing he saw was the shattered lamp lying in a pool of oil. A muffled knocking came from beneath the floor, and he threw himself at the cellar door, dragged back the heavy bolt and pulled it open. Corran climbed out, white with anger, and gripped his grandson so hard that Tam could hardly breathe.

Corran told them in a few harsh words that Drusk had done this, and that unless a light showed in the next few minutes, the ships would be upon the rocks. Vessa looked up at the great iron bowl on the tower, which was so huge that it needed the largest flame she had ever made, and old fear rose in her throat like a cold tide. She had practised small circles of fire in a cave, but this was a wild night, with the wind howling and the whole fleet depending on her aim.

Tam climbed the stairs behind her and stood at her side on the windy platform with his coat wrapped around his little candle, as if it were the most precious thing in the world. He did not tell her that it would be easy, because it would not be, and he did not tell her to be brave, because she already was. He only said that he was here, that he trusted her, and that all she had to do was to breathe out one breath at a time.

Vessa closed her eyes, filled her chest with the roaring wind, and let go of everything she had held back for eleven years. A great river of golden fire rushed out of her, poured into the iron bowl and burst upward in a column that lit the clouds from beneath, and not one spark strayed beyond the rim. It was the finest flame she had ever made, and she knew it, because it was not the flame of a dragon who was afraid.

Far out at sea, a shout went up from boat to boat as the great beacon blazed into life, for every sailor in the fleet knew that light better than he knew his own front door. They hauled on the tillers and wrenched their sails round, turning away from the wicked little lanterns and steering instead for the narrow channel that the true flame marked. Even the captain of the Gannet, who had never seen the dragon's fire before, sailed through the gap with his heart in his mouth.

Then Vessa dived from the tower like a falcon and skimmed low over the Teeth, where Drusk and his men were crouched in their boat, and she drew a ring of golden fire in the air all around them. It was a perfectly measured circle that scorched no one and yet left no doubt that she could have done a great deal more. The wreckers wailed, threw down their oars, and begged for mercy, while Captain Drusk sat in the middle of the flames with his coat on his knees and his mouth hanging open.

One by one the weary boats slid through the channel into the quiet water of the harbour, and the Gannet came last of all, riding low with her cargo and her crew singing on deck. The whole town had gathered on the quay in their coats and shawls, and when the last mooring rope had been tied, a cheer went up that rattled the windows of every house in Saltmere. Berrin Oakes, who had nearly lost his boat on the same rocks only a week before, was the first to shout the dragon's name.

The fishermen of Saltmere seized Drusk and his crew the moment their boat touched the quay, and the whole wicked plan came out before the town magistrate by midnight. Afterwards the people crowded around Vessa, who had landed gently among them, and Old Nan Tern was the first to tell her that the fire of that first week had been forgiven long ago. Vessa, who had carried that fire for eleven years like a stone in her heart, put her great head down onto the cobbles, and for a long time she did not move.

Winter came to Saltmere and went again, and every dusk the same small figure climbed the tower stairs beside the great blue-green dragon to watch her light the beacon. Her flame was never as wild as it had been that stormy night, nor as small as it had been in those fearful years, but just the right size for the work, bright and warm and steady. And the boats came home across the dark water, as they always would now, because a dragon had remembered that fire is not only a danger but a gift.
